title: ALU Design
summary: Building the arithmetic-logic unit and the flags every downstream branch and overflow check depends on.

slides.markdown:
The **Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)** is the component that actually computes — addition, subtraction, AND, OR, XOR, shifts, comparisons — selected by a **function code** the control unit derives from the opcode.

Structurally, it's just combinational logic: given two operands and a function-select signal, it produces a result (and, importantly, a set of status flags) with no memory of past operations. Every arithmetic and logic instruction in the ISA ultimately routes through this one shared block.

At its simplest, an ALU is an adder plus a handful of logic gates, with a **mux selecting which result to output**:

![A simple ALU: adder and logic gates feeding a mux selected by a function code](assets/simple-alu.svg)

Every operation — add, and, or — computes in parallel, and the function-select signal simply picks which computed result actually reaches the output. Wasteful in one sense (unused results are thrown away every cycle) but simple and fast, since nothing has to wait for a decision before computing.

assets.alt: A simple ALU: adder and logic gates feeding a mux selected by a function code

slides.markdown:
Alongside its numeric result, the ALU sets **condition flags**, side effects that later instructions read:

- **Zero** — set when the result is exactly 0; a conditional branch on equality reads this.
- **Negative** — set to the result's sign bit; feeds signed comparisons.
- **Carry** — set when unsigned addition overflows the register width; used for multi-word arithmetic and unsigned overflow checks.
- **Overflow** — set when signed addition/subtraction produces a mathematically wrong sign; feeds signed-overflow detection.

These flags are exactly how a comparison instruction "talks to" the branch that follows it — no separate channel, just shared flag bits.

The ALU doesn't need a separate subtractor circuit at all — **two's complement** makes `a - b` computable as `a + (~b + 1)`: invert `b`'s bits and add 1, then feed both into the *same* adder used for regular addition.

This is a direct hardware payoff of the two's complement representation ([signed-integer-representation](signed-integer-representation)): one adder plus a small inverter and a "+1" carry-in handles both operations, instead of building and wiring two separate circuits.

slides.sectionTitle: Adder design in the critical path
slides.markdown:
The adder inside the ALU sits on the CPU's **critical path** — the longest chain of logic the clock period must accommodate — so its internal design matters a lot:

| | Ripple-carry adder | Carry-lookahead adder |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Each bit's carry waits for the previous bit's carry | Carries computed in parallel from all input bits directly |
| Latency | Grows linearly with bit width — slow for 64-bit | Much lower, roughly logarithmic — but more gates |
| Hardware cost | Simple, small | More complex, larger |

Real CPUs use carry-lookahead (or hybrid) adders specifically because a slow adder directly caps the maximum clock speed — this is the ALU showing up as a first-order performance bottleneck, not an implementation detail.

A minimal ALU's function-select table, mapping a 3-bit selector to an operation:

```
ALUOp   Operation           Notes
000     A + B               ADD
001     A + (~B + 1)        SUB (via two's complement)
010     A AND B             bitwise AND
011     A OR B              bitwise OR
101     (A - B) < 0 ? 1 : 0 SLT (set-less-than, uses subtractor + sign bit)
```

Every real instruction's arithmetic (`add`, `sub`, `and`, `or`, `slt`) is just "pick the right 3-bit selector" — the control unit's job is exactly generating this selector from the opcode.

slides.subTitle: A worked example
slides.markdown:
```text
4-bit signed addition: 0111 (+7) + 0001 (+1)

  0111
+ 0001
------
  1000   <- result bit pattern

As unsigned: 1000 = 8 (no unsigned overflow, carry-out of MSB = 0)
As signed:   1000 = -8 in two's complement -- WRONG, should be +8

Overflow = carry INTO the sign bit (1, from bit 2 into bit 3)
           XOR carry OUT of the sign bit (0, out of bit 3)
         = 1 XOR 0 = 1  -> signed overflow flag set correctly
```

The hardware rule is exactly this XOR: signed overflow occurs precisely when the carry into the most significant bit differs from the carry out of it — a compact circuit computes this in parallel with the addition itself, no separate pass needed.

slides.sectionTitle: Multiply and divide live outside the simple ALU
slides.subTitle: Why they're multi-cycle
slides.markdown:
The add/sub/and/or ALU from earlier slides completes in one cycle, but **multiplication and division don't fit that mold**. A naive multiplier is a shift-and-add sequence — accumulate a partial product per bit of the multiplier — and a naive divider is an iterative shift-and-subtract, both taking many cycles for a wide operand rather than the fixed one-cycle latency of add/sub.

This is why multiply/divide are routed to dedicated, separate execution units, not folded into the same combinational block as the rest of the ALU: forcing every ALU operation to wait for the worst case (a full multi-cycle multiply) would slow down every single add and subtract too. Modern CPUs use fast multiplier arrays (Booth's algorithm, Wallace trees) to shrink multiply to a handful of cycles, but division remains stubbornly slower than every other arithmetic operation on essentially every architecture.

slides.subTitle: Carry flag vs overflow flag
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The carry flag and the overflow flag both mean 'the addition overflowed' — either one tells you the result is wrong."

**Why it's wrong:** they answer two **different** questions. The **carry flag** signals unsigned overflow — the result exceeded what fits unsigned in the register width. The **overflow flag** signals signed overflow — the result's sign is mathematically wrong for two's complement. The same addition can set one without the other: adding two large positive signed numbers can set overflow with carry clear, while adding two numbers that overflow unsigned range can set carry with overflow clear.

**Correct model:** check carry when your values are unsigned; check overflow when they're signed. Reading the wrong flag for your data's signedness produces a branch that looks plausible and is silently wrong — a classic source of hard-to-spot arithmetic bugs in low-level code.
